paragraphs: Mitya crossed the room with his long, quick strides and walked straight up to the table.

“Gentlemen,” he said in a loud voice, almost shouting, yet stammering over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—there’s nothing the matter,” he said, turning suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and gripped his hand tightly. “I ... I’m coming, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, for the last time, in this very room?”
He said the last words to the fat little man with the pipe, who sat on the sofa. The man took the pipe out of his mouth with dignity and said sternly:
“_Panie_, we’re here in private. There are other rooms.”
“Why, it’s you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What are you saying?” Kalganov suddenly answered. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“Delighted to see you, my dear ... my precious fellow. I always thought a lot of you.” Mitya answered joyfully and eagerly, and at once held out his hand across the table.
“Ow! How hard you squeeze! You’ve nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

“He always squeezes like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile. Mitya’s face had suddenly convinced her that he wasn’t going to make a scene. She was watching him with intense curiosity and some uneasiness still. Something about him impressed her, and in fact the last thing she had expected was that he would come in and speak like this at such a moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov ventured blandly on the left. Mitya rushed over to him, too.

“Good evening. You’re here, too! How glad I am to find you here, too! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned to the Polish gentleman with the pipe again, obviously taking him for the most important person present.) “I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room ... where I, too, adored ... my queen.... Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly, “I flew here and vowed— Oh, don’t be afraid, it’s my last night! Let’s drink to our good understanding. They’ll bring the wine at once.... I brought this with me.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a revel, like we had before. But the worm, the useless worm, will crawl away, and there’ll be no more of him. I will mark my day of joy on my last night.”

He was almost choking. He wanted to say so much, so much, but only strange exclamations came out. The Pole stared at him, then at the bundle of notes in his hand, then at Grushenka, and was clearly bewildered.
“If my suverin lady is permitting—” he began.

“What does ‘suverin’ mean? ‘Sovereign,’ I suppose?” Grushenka interrupted. “The way you talk, I can’t help laughing at you. Sit down, Mitya, what are you saying? Don’t frighten us, please. You won’t frighten us, will you? If you won’t, I’m glad to see you ...”
“Me, me frighten you?” cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won’t get in your way!...”

And suddenly he surprised them all, and no doubt himself as well. He threw himself onto a chair and burst into tears, turning his head to the opposite wall while his arms clasped the back of the chair tight, as though he were embracing it.

“Come, come, what a fellow you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That’s just how he comes to see me—he starts talking and I can’t make out what he means. He cried like that once before, and now he’s crying again! It’s shameful! Why are you crying? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added enigmatically, stressing each word with some irritation.
“I ... I’m not crying.... Well, good evening!” He instantly turned around in his chair and suddenly laughed—not his abrupt, wooden laugh, but a long, quivering, soundless nervous laugh.

“Well, there you go again.... Come, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka said to him coaxingly. “I’m very glad you’ve come, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I’m very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she said commandingly to the whole company, though her words were obviously meant for the man on the sofa. “I want it, I want it! And if he goes away, I’ll go, too!” she added, her eyes flashing.
“What my queen commands is law!” declared the Pole, gallantly kissing Grushenka’s hand. “I ask you, _panie_, to join our company,” he added politely to Mitya.
Mitya jumped up, obviously meaning to deliver another tirade, but the words wouldn’t come.
“Let’s drink, _panie_,” he blurted out instead of making a speech. Everyone laughed.

“Good heavens! I thought he was going to start again!” Grushenka exclaimed nervously. “Do you hear, Mitya,” she went on insistently, “don’t prance about, but it’s nice that you’ve brought champagne. I want some myself, and I can’t stand liqueurs. And best of all, you’ve come yourself. We were terribly dull here.... You’ve come for a spree again, I suppose? But put your money in your pocket. Where did you get so much?”

All this time Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and everyone’s eyes were fixed on it, especially the Poles’. In confusion he hurriedly stuffed it into his pocket. He flushed. At that moment the innkeeper brought in an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya snatched up the bottle, but he was so flustered that he didn’t know what to do with it. Kalganov took it from him and poured out the champagne.

“Another! Another bottle!” Mitya cried to the innkeeper. He forgot to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly invited to drink to their good understanding, and drank off his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face suddenly changed. The solemn, tragic expression he had come in with vanished completely, and something childlike came into his face. He seemed to have become suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked shyly and happily at everyone, with a steady nervous little laugh and the blissful look of a dog that has done wrong, been punished, and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, and looked around at everyone with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing all the while, and brought his chair close up to hers. Little by little he had formed some idea of the two Poles, though no definite conception of them yet.

The Pole on the sofa struck him by his dignified bearing and his Polish accent, and above all by his pipe. “Well, what of it? It’s a good thing he’s smoking a pipe,” he reflected. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and two very thin, pointed, dyed, impudent-looking mustaches, had not so far raised the faintest doubt in Mitya. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the Pole’s absurd wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks foolishly combed forward over the temples. “I suppose it’s all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, stared insolently and defiantly at the company and listened to the talk with silent contempt. He still impressed Mitya only by his great height, which was in striking contrast to the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s mind. It occurred to him, too, that this Pole must be the other’s friend, a sort of “bodyguard,” and that no doubt the big Pole was at the little Pole with the pipe’s disposal. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly right and beyond question. In his mood of doglike submissiveness, every feeling of rivalry had died away.

He completely failed to grasp Grushenka’s mood or the enigmatic tone of some of her words. All he understood, with a thrilling heart, was that she was kind to him, that she had forgiven him and made him sit by her. He was beside himself with delight, watching her sip her champagne. The silence of the company seemed to strike him, however, and he looked around at everyone with expectant eyes.
“Why are we sitting here, gentlemen? Why don’t you start doing something?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He keeps talking nonsense, and we were all laughing,” Kalganov began suddenly, as though he had guessed Mitya’s thought, and pointed to Maximov.
Mitya immediately stared at Kalganov and then at Maximov.
“He’s talking nonsense?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly seeming delighted at something—“ha ha!”
“Yes. Would you believe it, he insists that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. That’s awful rot, isn’t it?”
“Polish women?” repeated Mitya, utterly ecstatic.

Kalganov knew perfectly well how Mitya felt about Grushenka, and he guessed about the Pole, too. But that didn’t interest him much, maybe not at all; what interested him was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he was meeting the Poles at the inn for the first time in his life. He had known Grushenka before and had once gone to see her with someone, but she hadn’t taken to him. Tonight, though, she looked at him very affectionately. Before Mitya’s arrival she had been making much of him, but he seemed somehow unmoved by it. He was a boy, not over twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. Beautiful pale blue eyes looked out from that fair face, with an intelligent and sometimes even deep expression, beyond his age in fact, although the young man sometimes looked and talked quite like a child and was not at all ashamed of it, even when he knew it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Sometimes there was something fixed and obstinate in his expression. He would look at you and listen, seeming all the while to be dreaming stubbornly about something else. Often he was listless and lazy; at other times he would grow excited, sometimes, apparently, over the most trivial matters.

“Just imagine, I’ve been taking him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling indolently, quite naturally though, without the slightest affectation. “Ever since your brother, do you remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That made me take an interest in him then, and I took him with me to the country, but he keeps talking such rot that I’m ashamed to be with him. I’m taking him back.”
“The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is impossible,” the Pole with the pipe remarked to Maximov.
He spoke Russian fairly well, much better, anyway, than he pretended. When he used Russian words, he always twisted them into a Polish form.
“But I was married to a Polish lady myself,” tittered Maximov.
“But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov put in at once.
“A cavalry officer, really? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly and turning questioning eyes to each speaker, as though there was no knowing what he might hear from any of them.

“No, you see,” Maximov turned to him. “What I mean is that those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances a mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps on his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother look on and allow it.... They allow it ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and offers her his hand.... That’s how it is ... offers her his hand, he he!” Maximov ended, tittering.

“The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole on the chair growled suddenly, and crossed one leg over the other. Mitya’s eye was caught by his huge greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles’ clothes looked rather greasy.
“Well, now it’s _lajdak_! What is he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly vexed.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies of good birth,” the Pole with the pipe remarked to Grushenka.
“You can bet on that,” the tall Pole snapped contemptuously.
“What next! Let him talk! People talk, why stop them? It makes things cheerful,” Grushenka said crossly.
“I’m not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig. He gave Grushenka a long look, then lapsed into dignified silence and sucked his pipe again.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman spoke the truth.” Kalganov got excited again, as though it were a matter of vast importance. “He’s never been in Poland, so how can he talk about it? I suppose you weren’t married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Province of Smolensk. Only a Uhlan had brought her to Russia before that, my future wife, with her mamma and her aunt, and another female relation with a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. But he didn’t marry her, because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” cried Kalganov.
“Yes. They both deceived me a little at the time, and hid it. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun.”
“So glad she was going to marry you!” yelled Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

“Yes, so glad. But it turned out to be for quite a different reason. Afterwards, when we were married, after the wedding, that very evening, she confessed, and very touchingly asked forgiveness. ‘When I was a child I once jumped over a puddle,’ she said, ‘and hurt my leg.’ He he!”
Kalganov went off into the most childish laughter, almost falling onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed, too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

“Do you know, that’s the truth, he’s not lying now,” exclaimed Kalganov, turning to Mitya; “and do you know, he’s been married twice; it’s his first wife he’s talking about. But his second wife, do you know, ran away, and is alive now.”
“Is it possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov with a look of utter astonishment.

“Yes. She did run away. I’ve had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov modestly agreed, “with a _monsieur_. And what was worse, she’d had all my little property transferred to her beforehand. ‘You’re an educated man,’ she said to me. ‘You can always earn your living.’ That settled my business for her. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.’ He he!”

“Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he’s telling lies—and he often is—he’s only doing it to amuse us all. There’s no harm in that, is there? You know, I sometimes like him. He’s awfully low, but it’s natural to him, eh? Don’t you think so? Some people are low out of self-interest, but he’s simply that way by nature. Just imagine, he claims (he was arguing about it all the way yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Do you remember, there’s a landowner called Maximov in it, whom Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, do you remember, ‘for inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov in a drunken condition.’ Would you believe it, he claims that he was that Maximov and that he was beaten! Now, can that be so? Tchitchikov made his journey, at the very latest, at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don’t fit. He couldn’t have been thrashed then, could he?”
It was hard to imagine what Kalganov was so worked up about, but his excitement was genuine. Mitya followed his lead without protest.
“Well, but what if they did thrash him!” he cried, laughing.
“It’s not that they thrashed me exactly, but what I mean is—” put in Maximov.
“What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn’t.”
“What time is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, looking bored. The other shrugged his shoulders in reply. Neither of them had a watch.

“Why not talk? Let other people talk. Mustn’t other people talk because you’re bored?” Grushenka flew at him, plainly looking for a fault to find. Something seemed to flash across Mitya’s mind for the first time. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
“_Pani_, I didn’t object. I didn’t say anything.”
“All right then. Come, tell us your story,” Grushenka cried to Maximov. “Why is everyone silent?”

“There’s nothing to tell, it’s all so foolish,” Maximov answered at once, with obvious satisfaction, mincing a little. “Besides, all that’s by way of allegory in Gogol, for he’s given all the names a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name, he was called Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn’t an Italian but a Russian, and Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl with her pretty little legs in tights, and she had a little short skirt with spangles, and she kept turning round and round, only not for four hours but for four minutes only, and she bewitched everyone...”
“But what were you beaten for?” cried Kalganov.
“For Piron!” answered Maximov.
“What Piron?” cried Mitya.

“The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking then, a big party of us, in a tavern at that very fair. They’d invited me, and first of all I began quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny get-up!’ and Boileau answers that he’s going to a masquerade, that is, to the baths, he he! And they took it personally, so I hurried to repeat another, very sarcastic, well known to all educated people:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don’t know your way to the sea!

They were still more offended and began abusing me in the most unseemly way for it. And as bad luck would have it, to set things right I began telling a very cultured anecdote about Piron, how he was not accepted into the French Academy and, to avenge himself, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They seized me and thrashed me.”
“But what for? What for?”
“For my education. People can thrash a man for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
